drills.q: Define the iterator protocol precisely: what two methods, what does each return, and what signals completion?
drills.a: __iter__() returns an iterator (often self); __next__() returns the next value or raises StopIteration to signal completion.

drills.q: State precisely: is every iterator a generator? Is every generator an iterator? Give a concrete counterexample.
drills.a: Every generator is an iterator. Not every iterator is a generator — e.g. a hand-written class implementing __iter__/__next__, or a zip/file object, is an iterator with no yield anywhere.

drills.q: You write `gen = (x*x for x in range(5))` and then run `print(list(gen)); print(list(gen))`. What prints the second time, and why?
drills.a: [] the second time. The generator is exhausted after the first list() call; StopIteration fires immediately on the next next(), which list() silently interprets as zero items — no error is raised.

drills.q: Why does calling a generator function not execute any of its body immediately, even code before the first yield?
drills.a: Because any function containing yield anywhere is compiled as a generator function; calling it only constructs and returns a generator object. Execution begins only when next()/send() is first called on it.

drills.q: Explain what yield from adds beyond a plain `for x in sub: yield x` loop.
drills.a: yield from forwards send()/throw()/close() calls made on the outer generator into the sub-generator, and captures the sub-generator's return value as the result of the yield-from expression — a manual for-loop does neither.

drills.q: You call `g = my_gen(); g.send('hello')` on a freshly created generator. What happens and why?
drills.a: TypeError: can't send non-None value to a just-started generator. There is no suspended yield expression yet to receive the value; you must prime it with next(g) or g.send(None) first.

drills.q: You run itertools.groupby on data=[('a',1),('b',2),('a',3)] keyed by the first element, without sorting first. How many groups come out, and what are their keys?
drills.a: Three groups: 'a', 'b', 'a' — groupby only merges consecutive equal keys, and the second 'a' isn't adjacent to the first, so it starts a new group.

drills.q: When does itertools.tee stop being cheap, and what's the worst-case memory cost?
drills.a: When one of the resulting iterators is consumed much faster than another; tee must buffer every element the slower consumer hasn't reached yet, so in the worst case (one branch fully consumed before the other starts) the memory cost approaches that of materializing the entire sequence as a list.

drills.q: Give three concrete situations where reaching for a generator instead of a list is the wrong engineering call.
drills.a: Needing len() up front (progress reporting, preallocation); needing random access, indexing, or more than one pass over the data (retries, multi-statistic passes, multiple consumers); the dataset is small enough that materializing is essentially free and the generator only adds debugging friction.

drills.q: What does PEP 479 change about a StopIteration raised inside a generator's body, and what production bug did it fix?
drills.a: Since Python 3.7 it's enforced that an unhandled StopIteration escaping a generator's body is converted into a RuntimeError instead of propagating as-is. Before this, a stray StopIteration (e.g. from calling next() on an exhausted sub-iterator) would silently truncate whichever for-loop was consuming the outer generator, with no error at all.

drills.q: Design a memory-bounded pipeline that reads a 50GB log file and returns only the first line containing 'ERROR', without loading the file into memory. What's the peak memory profile?
drills.a: Chain a line-reading generator (iterating the file object directly, which reads one line at a time) into a filter/find function that returns on first match. Peak memory is one line at a time; if the match is near the top of the file, the rest is never read, unlike f.readlines() which loads everything up front regardless of where the match is.
